DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Verdict: not ready to send.** The recommendation is clearly stated, but one of its two proposals rests on a misreading of the paper's own table, and the headline numbers leave out a cost increase that the paper itself reports. The owners can check both points against the tables in front of them, so these need fixing before submission.

## 1. The risotto case contradicts Table 1

Section 5.2 says the mushroom risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows the opposite: at **80% it has the highest margin** of any main.

- **Cash profit per plate:** the risotto makes £11.20 (£14.00 − £2.80). That beats the chicken curry at £10.90, so it isn't the weakest on that measure either.
- **Sales:** at 90 plates a week it ties with specials for the lowest. "The lowest sales" is only half true.
- **Replacement margin:** specials currently average 64%. A special at the same price would earn about £200 a week *less* than the risotto (90 × £14 × 16 points).
- **Vegetarian option:** the risotto appears to be the only vegetarian main on the fixed menu. Replacing it with a rotating special affects groups that include a vegetarian, and that risk isn't mentioned.

There may still be a case for removing it, perhaps based on kitchen complexity, waste or prep time. But that case isn't in the paper, and the reason given is wrong. I'd recommend either making the real argument or dropping 5.2 from this paper.

## 2. The £42,000 and 71% figures ignore the beef increase

Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, but Section 5.3 doesn't account for it.

- **Profit impact:** if beef makes up most of the burger and steak food cost, the burger cost rises about £0.50 and the steak about £1.25. That's roughly **£280 a week** of extra cost against the £810 gain. Net of beef, the gain is nearer **£530 a week (about £27,500 a year)**.
- **Margin target:** I rebuilt the main-course margin from Table 1, assuming specials average about £16. Current margin is about 69%. The price rises alone reach about 71%, which matches the paper. After the beef increase it falls back to about **69%**, and the risotto swap pushes it slightly lower again. On these numbers the proposals offset rising costs rather than restoring the 70% target.

The arithmetic itself is right: 310 + 260 + 240 = £810, and × 52 = £42,120. The problem is that this is extra *revenue* at constant volume, not extra gross profit. It should be labelled that way, or the beef cost should be netted off.

## 3. Factual inconsistency

Section 8 says "across our six trading days a week." Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five days**. Fix whichever is wrong. If the restaurant closes for any weeks in the year, the × 52 annualisation also needs adjusting.

## 4. Dates are out of date

The paper is dated March 2026 and proposes changes from 1 April 2026. Today is 13 November 2026. If this is going to the owners now:
- the effective date needs updating;
- the January–February baseline is nine months old;
- the "notice" of a beef increase has presumably already taken effect.

The prices and volumes in Table 1 should be refreshed. If prices have already changed, the paper needs reframing.

## 5. Claims that need support or softening

- **"Volumes will hold"** is the assumption the whole projection rests on, and it's asserted rather than tested. A simple sensitivity line would help, e.g. "a 5% volume drop on the three dishes reduces the gain to £X."
- **"The 2024 change had no visible effect on bookings":** give the figures. Bookings also aren't the same as dish volumes, since guests can trade down to cheaper mains.
- **"Weekday lunch… a small share of main-course sales":** this isn't quantified. Friday and Saturday dinner is "just under half," so the rest is a large share. Fish and chips and burgers are likely lunch staples, so give the actual percentage.
- **Competitor position:** the midpoint claims are correct (fish £17.50 vs £17.98; burger £16.00 vs £16.50; steak £28.00 vs £29.50). However, all three dishes would move from cheapest in the group to above the lowest competitor. "Competitively priced" is fair. "The value option," as in your covering note, is less clearly true.

## 6. Monitoring plan needs a trigger and a fair baseline

- **Baseline:** comparing April–May volumes to January–February will likely show a seasonal rise that hides any price-driven drop. Compare against April–May 2025, or track each dish's share of total mains.
- **Trigger:** state what happens if volumes fall, e.g. "if any dish falls more than X% against baseline, we will review its price at week 8." Without that, the eight weeks give no early warning.

## Smaller points

- Section 1 cites the *overall* food margin (70% → 67%), but the proposals only cover mains. One sentence linking the two would help.
- UK menu prices include VAT. If the margins are calculated on VAT-inclusive prices, they overstate true gross margin. Check this is consistent with how the 70% target is defined.

## Suggested path to ready

1. Correct or remove the risotto proposal.
2. Net the beef cost increase out of 5.3 and restate the margin outcome.
3. Fix "six trading days" and update the dates and data.
4. Add a volume sensitivity line and a monitoring trigger.

After these changes the price-increase proposal would still be reasonable and well-supported. It would just be presented accurately.
